topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

outline.topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Language
sections.content: Introduce binary as a base-2 system. Explain that just as decimal uses 10 digits (0-9), binary uses only 0 and 1, where each position represents a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8...).
sections.example: Visual: A row of 4 light bulbs. Each bulb represents a bit. Bulb ON = 1, Bulb OFF = 0. Show how 1011 in binary equals 8+0+2+1 = 11 in decimal.

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle
sections.content: Define the classic puzzle: 3 rods and n discs of different sizes. Rules: Move one disc at a time, never place a larger disc on a smaller one. The goal is to move the full stack to a target rod.
sections.example: Visual: 3 discs on Peg A. Animation shows the sequence of moves required to shift the stack to Peg C, emphasizing the recursive nature of the puzzle.

sections.title: Mapping Moves to Binary Codes
sections.content: Explain the surprising link: If we number the moves from 1 to 2^n - 1, the disc to be moved corresponds to the position of the lowest set bit in the binary representation of the move number.
sections.example: Visual: A table comparing Move Number (1-7), its Binary form (001, 010, 011...), and the disc to move (Disc 1, 2, 1, 3...). Use a character, 'Robo-Solver', pointing at the specific disc for each step.

sections.title: The Binary Direction Rule
sections.content: Define the direction of the moves based on binary state. For odd discs, moves go in a specific cycle; for even discs, the opposite cycle.
sections.example: Visual: 'Disk-o-Bot' moves Disc 1 (the smallest) clockwise among pegs, while larger discs follow a fixed parity rule based on their binary index, ensuring the puzzle is solved automatically.

sections.title: Summary and Real-world Application
sections.content: Synthesize the concept: The puzzle is a physical manifestation of a binary counter. This logic is fundamental to recursive programming and algorithm complexity analysis.
sections.example: Visual: A final graphic showing a computer processor's clock cycle (0s and 1s) evolving into the movement of Hanoi discs, demonstrating how counting sequences drive mechanical movement.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Language
lecture_lines: Binary systems use only two digits: zero and one.
Each position represents an increasing power of two.
Four bits can represent numbers from zero to fifteen.
Binary is the language of all modern computers.
[Asset: light_bulbs_animation]
animations: Display bit string '001' at center; color #FFFFFF.
Flash '001' in #FFD700 to emphasize bit length.

storyboard.title: The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle
lecture_lines: The puzzle has three rods and stacked discs.
Move one disc at a time between rods.
Never place a larger disc on a smaller one.
The goal is moving all discs to another rod.
[Asset: hanoi_puzzle_setup]
animations: Highlight largest disk at bottom of tower A.
Animate move of largest disk to tower C.

storyboard.title: Mapping Moves to Binary Codes
lecture_lines: We label moves from one to two power n.
Binary digits map directly to disc moves.
The lowest set bit determines which disc moves.
[Asset: binary_mapping_table]
animations: Connect disks and bits with #808080 lines.

storyboard.title: The Binary Direction Rule
lecture_lines: Smallest discs follow a strict cyclic pattern.
Larger discs move based on binary parity rules.
This ensures the puzzle is always solved correctly.
[Asset: robot_disc_path]
animations: Show rule: '0 = move right', '1 = move left'.
Animate disk movement following these directions.

storyboard.title: Summary and Real-world Application
lecture_lines: The puzzle acts like a simple binary counter.
Binary logic governs complex recursive algorithms.
Counting cycles drive fundamental computer processes.
